data.title: My adult kids are big earners. Should I do a Roth conversion now so they aren't taxed as much on their inheritance?
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

Inherited IRAs can create a tax liability for heirs, but this should not be your first concern

It can be hard to decide which way to go on a Roth conversion in retirement.

Got a question about retirement? Fill out our new questionnaire or write to me directly at beth.pinsker@marketwatch.com (please put "Fix My Portfolio" in the subject line).

Dear Fix My Portfolio,

Our two children and their spouses are big earners, and I'm thinking about what we might leave behind to them. I'm 70 and have started Social Security already, and my spouse is 66 and is waiting until 70 to claim. I have a handle on Medicare surcharges and the $6,000 senior additional deduction rules. We keep our income under the New Jersey limit for tax-sheltered income, which results in no state tax for us. Whatever is left is in tax-sheltered accounts that would go to the kids and be highly taxed as opposed to our tax rate. An inherited IRA complicates the Roth solution during this period between retirement and required minimum distributions. I want to know that I have not missed something tax-wise.

Thinking Ahead

Dear Thinking Ahead,

You are definitely on the ball. You are thinking through all the conditions you should to figure out if and when you should do a Roth conversion. Perhaps what you are missing is patience.

I understand the urge to do something. You indicated in your answers to our new MarketWatch Retirement Questionnaire that you're managing your money on your own and are keeping track of most of your accounts either on your workplace retirement plan's web interface or on your own spreadsheet. This is a high level of engagement that should serve you well. You're also seeking out answers and trying to think ahead. All of this is exactly what it takes to successfully execute your retirement plan.

When retirees arrive at this place where they have everything mapped out and now it's time to just work the plan, they can get stymied. You think you're supposed to be doing something, but it's possible that what you should be doing is just proceeding onward as planned.

The worry you have about your tax rates versus the tax rates of your heirs is legitimate, but it doesn't necessarily need to be acted on right now. You and your spouse are still young. You should be considering your tax rate now versus your future tax rate, before you think about your future tax rate versus your children's. The former has one known factor - your current tax rate - while the latter has two unknowns.

In these years before you start taking required minimum distributions, which will be at age 73 for you and 75 for your spouse, Roth conversions could well make sense for you. It's possible - even likely - that your coming RMDs would push you into a higher tax bracket, and this kind of move would give you more options for tax diversification.

Say, for example, that you are in the 12% or 22% bracket now, with earnings below $211,400. That would keep you below the married threshold for the Medicare surcharges known as IRMAA. But once you start taking RMDs, even just a little extra income could push you beyond the $218,000 IRMAA cliff where the extra monthly charges start. Plus you'll pay income tax on your pretax distributions.

This is why financial advisers use the window between retirement and the start of RMDs to do multiyear Roth conversions. You can do this on your own with your spreadsheets or use do-it-yourself planning software. The key is to map out where you are in your current tax bracket and where RMDs will push you in the future. Then look at your available cash on hand to pay the extra tax due. If you can make use of the $6,000 extra senior deduction for both you and your spouse, all the better. That can offset some or all of the cost, and you can dig less deeply into your cash reserves to fund the conversion.

Thinking about your children

Once you settle all that, then you can think about your adult children. It might be a few years down the road before you act on this, however. Some retirees get to a point where their health is deteriorating or they are reaching very advanced ages and they can more clearly see what will be left after they die. At that point, you will have already secured what you need for your own living expenses and, potentially, your long-term-care needs, because you'll know the cards you've been dealt.

That's when you can think about ripping off the bandage and converting funds to Roth with an eye to the tax rate of the next generation. If you're still in the 24% bracket in 10 years, but your kids are steadily in the 32% or higher brackets, then it might make sense to convert over several years. It doesn't matter what those brackets are, as long as their bracket is above your bracket.

In his book "The Inheritance Playbook," Chad Holmes gives the example of parents who are in their 80s and have $894,000 in a tax-deferred IRA. They are in the 12% bracket, and their daughter is in the 22% bracket. If that money passes to the daughter, and she moves it to a brokerage steadily over the course of 10 years, as required, it's only worth $698,000 to her. If the parents convert it over six years, however, they'd pay $65,000 in tax and the daughter would inherit $1.1 million in a Roth account. "That would be roughly $195,000 in tax savings just by implementing some advanced tax strategies," Holmes wrote.

This may yet be something you try out, but perhaps just not right now. So all you're missing tax-wise is discipline and patience. Meanwhile, continue to keep an eye on your accounts and wait for your moment to act.

You can also join the Retirement conversation in our Facebook community: Retire Better with MarketWatch.

By submitting your story to Dow Jones & Co., the publisher of MarketWatch, you understand and agree that we may use your story, or versions of it, in all media and platforms, including via third parties.

-Beth Pinsker

data.title: My brother asked me to sign as his executor, but wouldn't let me read the document. Should I have refused?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I imagine scenarios like this happen more often than people realize'

"This situation does not seem ideal." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

Years ago, my husband's sister called and asked me to be the executor of her estate. She explained why she had chosen me and gave me specific instructions about how she wanted certain things handled.

A few weeks later, she emailed me what appeared to be a copy of her will, but it was unsigned. It was very straightforward and didn't include any of the details she had discussed with me over the phone.

A few years later, my husband told me that I was no longer the executor. My sister-in-law had become close to a new friend - her tenant - and had decided this person would be a better choice.

Around the same time, my brother asked me to be the executor of his estate. He had me sign the last page of what appeared to be his will, but he didn't want me to read any of it. I don't have a copy, and I have no idea where it would be if I ever needed to find it.

This situation does not seem ideal. Was I ever really my sister-in-law's executor if I never signed anything and only received an unsigned copy of the will? And if my brother dies, do I tell someone that years ago I signed something naming me as executor?

I imagine scenarios like this happen more often than people realize. Gosh, I hope I go first.

Uncertain Executor

Related: My ex-husband's sister died - so why is Fidelity asking me for her death certificate?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

You might have signed away your rights to your parents' inheritance.

Dear Uncertain,

Your sister-in-law may just be a bit flaky. Your brother, however, acted very suspiciously.

Being named as executor is not the same as actually becoming executor. Your sister-in-law could have nominated you in her will without having you sign anything. You would only become executor if she died with that will in effect, and the probate court appointed you.

You never signed legal paperwork agreeing to be your sister-in-law's executor (or executrix). For that reason, treat it as a wash. She asked you. It was nice to be asked, and your husband "unasked" you on her behalf.

In many U.S. jurisdictions, an executor is named in a person's will, not by signing an acceptance beforehand. The executor typically accepts or declines the appointment after the "testator" dies and the probate court opens administration of the estate.

Was it the most elegant way of handling the situation? Nope. Has your sister-in-law, for better or for worse, saved you an awful lot of time and work that goes into being an executor? Absolutely. It's a thankless job, and one that also comes with legal jeopardy.

Forgive me for being an alarmist, but your brother's document gives me pause. He asked you to be his executor and you signed an acceptance of appointment (sometimes called an acceptance of executorship). He did not allow you to read the document.

There is no sensitive financial and/or estate-planning information in such a document, so I don't understand why he would not allow you to read it. (Usually, it will have his name, Social Security Number and date of birth etc.)

It's not like he didn't want you to, say, read his will or bank accounts or 401(k) transcript. What bothers me is that you signed a document - we don't even know if it was an acceptance of appointment - without reading it. Frankly, you could have signed anything.

You might have signed away your rights to your parents inheritance; a power of attorney, giving him authority over your finances or legal affairs; a deed or quitclaim deed transferring ownership of real estate; or even a beneficiary designation or trust document.

Related: Should wealthier Americans forgo their Social Security benefits as a charitable gesture?

Declining the role

You should never sign a legal document if you are told not to read it, rushed or pressured to sign, or if the title of the document does not match the explanation or has suspicious blank spaces left to be filled in later.

There's no way to know from your description exactly what you signed, and that's precisely why it's never advisable to sign any legal document you haven't reviewed. I don't know your brother, but I do know - from letters to this column - that people do the oddest things.

If your brother did have you sign a document you could alert the probate court - if he predeceased you - to decline the role. You cannot be compelled to serve as an executor, even if you're named in someone's will.

The appointment is a nomination, not a legal obligation, and you are free to change your mind. If you choose not to serve, it's best to do so promptly so the estate can be administered without unnecessary delay.

There are many reasons to decline, including living far away, health issues, conflicts of interest, or simply lacking the time or ability to manage the estate. It's more common than many people realize, and being named as executor does not obligate you to accept the role.

If you decline before the court appoints you, you simply do not file a petition for letters testamentary. You have no legal duty to step forward, although you should notify the beneficiaries and any alternate executors named in the will as soon as possible.

In your situation, the simplest course would be to decline the appointment after your brother's death (assuming your brother predeceases you). That approach avoids unnecessary conflict during her lifetime while preserving your right to step aside when the time comes.

Probate typically takes four to 12 months, and executors are usually entitled to reasonable compensation, often 1% to 3% of the estate (but this varies enormously by state and estate). Keep that in mind before you make your final decision about taking on this role.

And, my friend, please don't sign a document without reading it again.

data.title: 'This has been an emotionally difficult time': My brother has cancer and my father is 94. How do I shoulder this responsibility?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'My father placed his $600,000 Wisconsin home into a revocable trust, naming my brother as beneficiary'

"If my niece and her mother continue living in the home, are there any special tax or trust considerations?" (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

Over 20 years ago, my father placed his $600,000 Wisconsin home into a revocable trust, naming my brother as beneficiary. I am now co-trustee with my father. This has been an emotionally difficult time.

My brother has advanced cancer with a poor prognosis. We amended the trust so that if my brother predeceases my 94-year-old father, his inheritance passes to his 19-year-old daughter. The trust also provides that the house (or proceeds) remains in trust until my niece turns 25.

My questions:

-- After my father dies, will the trust need its own Employer Identification Number (EIN) even if the house is not sold?

-- If my niece and her mother continue living in the home, are there any special tax or trust considerations?

-- If the home is sold before my niece turns 25, I assume the proceeds would remain in a trust account?

We have an appointment with our estate attorney, but I would appreciate any general guidance.

My brother has very few assets outside the trust. We are also updating his estate-planning documents, and he plans to name my niece as his primary financial and healthcare agent, with her mother and me as backups.

I am the closest family member, so I've been taking my brother to treatments, helping manage his care and maintaining his property. If I lose both my father and brother in a short period, I expect to be responsible for administering the trust and managing the house for my niece.

Fortunately, I have a close relationship with both my niece and her mother, and I've also been able to help support my niece's education through a 529 plan established when she was born.

Thank you for any insights in trying to be all things to all people.

Son & Brother

Related: 'He's never been good with money': If I set up an annuity for my brother, 65, would it jeopardize his Supplemental Security Income?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

If they're living in the house rent-free, there won't be rental income to report and, as such, no taxes.

Dear Son & Brother,

Make sure you don't end up holding up everybody else's world. You're dealing with a lot: the potential loss of your brother and the collective and personal grief if he dies before your aging father, in addition to the financial responsibility of managing this $600,000 trust.

The biggest takeaway from your letter is that you can't deal with all of this alone. You need a team, and you certainly need an accountant and a trust-and-estate attorney to help you navigate the trust and the house contained in the trust.

With your brother's illness, you are shouldering a physical, emotional and legal burden. You may already be grieving the possibility of loss while your brother is still here and while you are actively helping him through his exhaustive cancer treatment.

Everyone has limits and there's no shame in that.

This is the kind of situation where you can learn to lean on others - family and friends, or even a support group, a counselor, clergy or a caregiving network - before you reach your breaking point. This could be a years-long process and you also need to protect your mental health.

Know your limits. Everyone has them, and there's no shame in that. If you do become trustee, you must follow the trust terms and act in your niece's best interests - and resist being the receptacle for endless familial requests.

Carrying the weight for a sibling and parent comes from a place of love and duty, but doing too much can lead to burnout. Being a dependable family member often means putting your own needs after other people's problems.

Decide which legal tasks you are able to manage, and communicate those limits to your family and trust-and-estate lawyer. Setting boundaries with others is not a selfish act. On the contrary, it helps ensure that you can continue to be present.

Related: 'Her bank accounts were stripped bare by Medicaid': My late friend had $20,000 in credit-card debt. Will her life insurance pay for it?

When the trust becomes irrevocable

To answer your other questions: The trust will require its own EIN for tax returns. While your father is alive, his revocable living trust is generally treated as a grantor trust, so it uses his Social Security number and doesn't file a separate fiduciary income-tax return.

When your father passes away, the trust then becomes irrevocable and obtains its own EIN - allowing you to open trust financial accounts under that EIN, which is linked to the trust rather than whether the house is sold or not.

There will almost always be tax considerations depending on who lives in a family home - relatives, beneficiaries or tenants - as long as the trust allows your niece and her mother to continue living in the home and you agree on property taxes, insurance and maintenance.

When your father dies, the trust becomes irrevocable.

If your niece's mother lives there rent-free, the trustee should be comfortable that doing so benefits your niece and there should be no rules forbidding it. If they're living in the house rent-free, there won't be rental income to report and, as such, no taxes.

If the trust requires the proceeds to remain in trust until your niece hits 25, the sale proceeds stay titled in the trust and are invested in trust-owned accounts. Any investment income - interest, dividends, capital gains, etc. - is reported by the trust.

Single individual filers do not reach the top 37% federal income-tax bracket until taxable income exceeds $640,600. In contrast, a nongrantor trust reaches the 37% top rate on undistributed taxable income above just $16,000.

"Trusts can be effective tools to help manage and protect your assets and may reduce or even eliminate costs related to wealth transfer, such as probate fees and gift and estate taxes," according to Fidelity. "But there are trade-offs to consider."

Have a team, and don't forget about your own needs.

Related: 'Her bank accounts were stripped bare by Medicaid': My late friend had $20,000 in credit-card debt. Will her life insurance pay for it?

data.title: The size of the American workforce has fallen by over 1 million people in the past year. Here's what's going on.
data.description:
By Andrew Keshner

The labor-force participation rate has been skidding for months

What's going on with the job hunt these days?

The share of Americans who are working or looking for a job hasn't been this low since the pandemic, according to a July jobs report full of gut punches.

It's a signal of shifting demographics and a sign of the current mood, economists said - and it's causing some worry.

The labor-force participation rate measures the share of people who are potentially available for work and either pulling in paychecks or out there looking for a job.

That rate fell to 61.4%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Friday. February 2021 was the last time the rate was so low.

"Declines in the participation rate are becoming more concerning, as it's currently near historic lows," Dominic Pappalardo, Morningstar Wealth's chief multi-asset strategist, said in a note.

Setting aside the pandemic, the participation rate hasn't been this low in decades, Pappalardo said.

A declining share of people who are ready to work presents a challenge for long-term economic growth, said Cory Stahle, senior economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab.

The size of the workforce has fallen by over 1 million people in the past year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It's now 169.1 million, compared with 170.4 million last July, according to agency data. The biggest decline occurred in the last couple of months.

It's just one report, and hiring in the summer can be tricky. But experts say there are several forces pushing the rate lower.

First is the ongoing retirement of baby boomers. The youngest boomers are now in their early 60s, and their continuing departure from the workforce is "the most steady thing pushing [the rate] lower. That's the clear, sustained decline," said Stahle.

There's also the birth rate, which has been declining for years, as well as tighter immigration rules and increased enforcement during President Donald Trump's second term, said Matthew Martin, senior U.S. economist at Oxford Economics. As older workers continue their large-scale exit from the workforce, "we don't necessarily have other additional young workers to fill their spot," he said.

The waning labor-force participation rate is also likely a reflection of job hunters' rising frustrations as they try to find work.

The BLS counts someone as actively looking for work if they've applied for jobs in the past four weeks.

In today's sluggish hiring environment, that four-week period could amount to a heartbeat. The July jobs report showed it took unemployed Americans almost 25 weeks on average to find their next job. Around one-quarter of unemployed job seekers have been on the hunt for at least half a year.

So it's possible that after a person sent out scores of applications with no reply, they took a break from looking - and that would technically push them out of the labor pool, said Stahle.

There were 503,000 "discouraged workers" in July, up from nearly 460,000 a year ago, according to the BLS. This category of people did not look for work in the past four weeks, and their reasons could include thinking that no work was available.

It's possible those demoralized job seekers are pushing the participation rate lower, said Martin of Oxford Economics. "I don't know if that's noise in the data, or the start of a trend," he said. "That definitely could be a piece of it."

As Stahle sees it, stymied job seekers are showing in the numbers. "The fear here is we move to a state where people say 'I'm no longer looking,'" Stahle told MarketWatch. "I'm just kind of giving up on my job search right now."

-Andrew Keshner

How Morikol® Tripeptides Support Joint, Skin, and Hair Wellness in PureHealth Research Peptide Supplements

PR Newswire

MANASSAS, Va., Aug. 8, 2026

MANASSAS, Va., Aug. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- PureHealth Research is spotlighting the growing consumer interest in peptide nutrition and the role thoughtful nutritional choices play in maintaining healthy joints, skin and hair. Many of today's peptide supplements feature Morikol® Marine Collagen Tripeptides, a premium collagen ingredient frequently included in formulations designed to help maintain structural wellness and healthy aging.

data.title: 'My head hit the driver's window': A teenager T-boned our car. Will Medicare pay my hospital bills?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'My car was nearly 20 years old, and I only carried liability and uninsured motorist coverage, not collision coverage'

"I'm basically in a holding pattern." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My wife and I are both on Medicare. She is 67 and works part-time; I'm 69 and still work full-time. We were recently involved in a car accident when a teenage driver ran a stop sign and struck our car directly in the driver's door.

My head hit the driver's window pretty hard, and my wife injured her wrist. The fire department responded and checked our blood pressure and pulse, but both vehicles had to be towed from the scene.

The next day, I saw my primary-care doctor. Because of my age and some existing health conditions, he was concerned about the possibility of a brain bleed and sent me to the ER for a CT scan of my head, and X-rays of my shoulder.

At the ER, I told them my injuries were the result of a motor-vehicle accident, and I used my Medicare coverage for the visit. I'm hoping you can explain how Medicare works in a situation like this when the other driver is at fault. I'm planning to start physical therapy.

The accident report hasn't been posted yet. The state trooper told me the other driver was at fault. I contacted the other driver's insurance company, and they said they're waiting for the accident report before moving forward - so I'm basically in a holding pattern.

My car was nearly 20 years old, and I only carried liability and uninsured motorist coverage, not collision. My insurance company told me to work directly with the other driver's insurance company regarding the damage to my vehicle.

Should I continue using Medicare for treatment? Does the other driver's auto insurance pay first, or does Medicare? Do I need to tell the hospital to bill someone other than Medicare? Will Medicare seek reimbursement later if the other driver's insurance settles the claim?

The Driver

Related: My wife's 2011 Ford Fiesta was totaled. Should we accept a $2,000 insurance settlement or give up the car for $2,700?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

If you later receive a settlement from the teen driver's insurance company, Medicare would be reimbursed for any conditional payments it made in the immediate aftermath of the car accident.

Dear Driver,

You need the three Ps: patience, paperwork and perseverance.

Conditional payments are standard practice and allow you to receive medical care, like CT scans and X-rays.

When someone else is at fault for an automobile accident, Medicare can pay your accident-related medical bills if the liability insurer isn't paying promptly, so you don't have to delay treatment or pay the bills yourself while the claim is pending. In this case, the teenage driver's insurance is still processing the claim.

In accidents like yours, there is a "primary" payer and a "secondary" payer. If the teenage driver's insurance company is legally responsible for your medical bills, it is the primary payer, and Medicare is the secondary payer. However, if the auto insurer can't or won't pay promptly, Medicare will make conditional payments for your covered medical bills.

If you later receive a settlement or court judgment from the teenage driver's insurer, Medicare would typically be reimbursed for any conditional payments it made in the aftermath of the automobile accident. If you receive a settlement, Medicare is generally reimbursed from those settlement proceeds.

Contact Medicare's Benefits Coordination & Recovery Center (BCRC). Medicare will calculate the amount that must be repaid. You can also call the BCRC toll-free at 1-855-798-2627 or report the accident online using the Medicare Secondary Payor Recovery Portal, providing your full name, Medicare number, date of birth and the accident details.

Don't miss: My ex-husband's sister died - so why is Fidelity asking me for her death certificate?

Automobile insurance

Given that you don't have collision insurance, your insurance will not pay for the totaled car. Therefore, the teenage driver's insurance company would be responsible for paying for your car, if they are found liable. The state trooper reportedly said the other driver was at fault, but the at-fault drivers' insurer is waiting for the official report before accepting liability.

Assuming the third-party driver's insurance company accepts responsibility, the insurer would normally pay the "actual cash value" of your car if it's declared a total loss. Fair warning: Your car was nearly 20 years old, so any payment will be based on its fair market value before the accident, and not the cost for replacing your car after the accident.

If the other driver's insurer denies liability or disputes the claim, you may have to negotiate with them, file a complaint if appropriate, or even pursue legal action. (Under the circumstances, that may cost you more money than the car was actually worth.) Wait for the other driver's insurance company to complete its investigation and determine liability.

In some states, first-party medical benefits such as Personal Injury Protection (PIP) or Medical Payments (MedPay) coverage may pay before Medicare, but rules vary by state, and not every state requires PIP or MedPay coverage. Some states require PIP with minimums like $5,000 or $10,000. Others require more or have no PIP requirement.

Thankfully, the teenage driver has insurance. If the teenage driver had been uninsured, your collision coverage would not have applied because you don't carry it. Instead, you would have had to rely on any uninsured motorist property damage (UMPD) coverage included in your policy or pursue the driver directly, or pursue the driver for damages.

The at-fault driver does have insurance. That's 99% of the battle.

data.title: Paying for pricey daycare? Here's how to keep saving for retirement at the same time.
data.description:
By Alessandra Malito

Young families are striving to do better but struggling with costs of living, including expensive childcare

Childcare can be expensive, and a barrier to other major financial goals like saving for retirement.

Many parents are in a conundrum: They need their jobs to pay the bills, but they also need trustworthy childcare; without the latter, they may not be able to work those jobs. Young families are struggling with the balance.

Add in the pressure of needing to pay or save for other major financial goals, such as retirement, and it might feel almost impossible. Parents across all income groups feel the stress of trying to do it all, said Dom Williams, a senior expert at McKinsey & Co. and a key author of a new McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility report.

In fact, Americans of all ages, backgrounds and incomes are striving for a better life, but say rising costs of living are keeping them from their aspirations, the researchers found. The McKinsey report was based on a survey of more than 30,000 Americans in all 50 states.

Childcare, which has increased in cost dramatically in recent years, presents a particular burden. "As you have the capacity to spend towards childcare, then you are exposed to the cost of childcare," Williams said.

The trade-offs for many parents are to either continue to work and pay - sometimes thousands of dollars a month - for childcare, or leave the workforce to take on caregiving responsibilities. The alternative to outsourced childcare has a few invisible price tags, however; leaving a job not only cuts off a source of income for present-day expenses, but also the ability to save for the future.

The challenge of childcare

Childcare can easily eat away at a family's budget. The average weekly daycare cost is $332 and the average weekly nanny cost is $870, according to the Care.com 2026 Cost of Care report. That equates to more than $17,000 a year for daycare or more than $45,000 a year for a nanny. Childcare accounts for 20% or more of the average parent's annual income, and more than 3 in 10 (31%) parents are dipping into their savings to pay for it, the Care.com research found.

"Childcare and retirement savings don't have to compete if you automate the retirement piece first," said Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner and managing partner at Chesapeake Financial Planners. "The years you're paying for daycare are usually your highest-earning years too, which is exactly why quitting on retirement now costs more later."

Judge had a client last year where both spouses were working and they were paying more for daycare than their mortgage. They were going to stop 401(k) contributions altogether, he recalled, but instead he worked with them to cut down the contribution rate to the amount that captured the full employer match "and nothing more."

"Below that threshold, you're leaving free money on the table, and free money is the one thing a young family with childcare bills genuinely cannot afford to skip," Judge said. "Above it, during the daycare years, is optional. Automate the number that survives the childcare years."

Childcare is 'temporary'

One of the most important things parents can remember when they're stressed about paying for childcare while funding their other financial goals is that childcare, while expensive, is a temporary line item on the budget, financial advisers noted.

Jon Ulin, a certified financial planner and managing principal of Ulin & Co. Wealth Management, said he and his wife have experienced the puzzle of childcare - including using daycare, a part-time nanny, help from family members and flexible work schedules.

"It wasn't always easy, but we treated childcare as a temporary investment rather than a permanent expense," Ulin said. "The challenge is building a plan that gets you through those years without sacrificing your long-term financial future. Sometimes, the best financial decision is paying for childcare."

The alternative is having one parent leave the workforce, which would cause a disruption in his or her career, as well as halt savings with employer matches in retirement accounts or contributions to Social Security that are linked to future benefits.

"Too many families compare this month's daycare bill instead of the lifetime earnings they are protecting," Ulin said. "The answer usually isn't finding an extra $1,500 a month; it's making five or six decisions that each free up $200 to $300 a month. Families who successfully balance childcare and retirement rarely make one dramatic change. They make a series of temporary trade-offs until childcare is behind them."

Ulin suggests a few ways to free up extra cash in the budget until childcare is no longer necessary, including: shopping around for the best insurance rates; refinancing debt to have lower fixed bills; delaying lifestyle upgrades, like a new car or an expensive vacation; and splitting any raises between savings for childcare and the future before spending it elsewhere. There are also tax benefits to look out for, including the child- and dependent-care tax credit, or dependent-care FSAs that allow for childcare costs to be paid with pretax dollars.

See also: How parents can take advantage of the 'best summer-camp tax break in years'

What to plan for next

Treat the last day of childcare as a raise, advisers said.

When the last bill is paid, instead of taking it as extra cash to spend in the present, automate savings for retirement and other big financial goals. Avoid lifestyle creep, where seeing more money in the checking account is tied to the feeling of more freedom to spend.

"As children get older, enter public school or no longer need full-time care, don't let that extra cash quietly disappear into day-to-day spending," said Kate Feeney, a certified financial planner and vice president at Summit Place Financial Advisors. "Treat the reduction in childcare expenses like a raise you've already committed to your future. This is one of the most powerful ways to avoid lifestyle creep and can meaningfully improve your long-term financial security."

-Alessandra Malito

data.title: 'My wife and I are both retired': Do we dip into our $2.3 million fund to pay off our $300,000 mortgage at 2.9%?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'Right now, we're withdrawing about $100,000 a year from our investments'

"Our home is worth $1.3 million." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

I would appreciate some input on whether it makes sense to pay off our mortgage. My wife and I are both retired. We have approximately $2.3 million in savings and investments, with about 90% invested in equities. I'm 65, and she's 58.

Our home is worth $1.3 million, and we still owe approximately $300,000 on the mortgage. The interest rate is a fixed 2.9%, and our monthly payment for property taxes, insurance and HOA dues are about $1,300 a month.

Right now, we're withdrawing about $100,000 a year from our investments. Once we begin collecting Social Security and our pensions, we'll receive about $110,000 annually, which should cover our living expenses.

Our other major costs are $1,200 a month for my wife's COBRA coverage, $350 a month for my Medicare and $238 a month for other insurance. Given our situation, does it make sense to pay off the remaining balance on the mortgage?

Tempted To Go Debt Free

Related: 'I've plenty of time on my hands': Advisers bombard me with offers of free steak dinners. Is it wrong to go for the food?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually,

It's a no-brainer. Keep the mortgage, and keep those stocks.

Dear Tempted,

The clue is in the question.

Historically, diversified stock portfolios have generated average annual returns of roughly 7% to 10% over long periods. A 2.9% mortgage is a guaranteed cost. If your mortgage rate was 7%-10%, and you were only getting 2.9% on your investments, I'd say, "Sure, pay off the mortgage. Your investment returns are not even keeping up with inflation." But with your current state of affairs? It's a no-brainer. Keep the mortgage, and keep those stocks.

From a purely financial standpoint, keeping your money invested is likely the better choice. You actually have three options: pay off the mortgage, continue making your regular mortgage payments or pay down part of the mortgage to reduce your monthly expenses. Paying off the mortgage also ties up $300,000 in home equity. You would have to sell the home, refinance or open a home-equity line of credit to release it again.

To play devil's advocate: You would save nearly $100,000 in interest over the next 20 years by paying off your mortgage. Some people yearn for zero debt, so your decision isn't strictly about the numbers - as compelling as they are - it's also about your risk tolerance as you enjoy your retirement. History shows the long-term growth trajectory is that your house will increase in value. Ditto, the stock market, despite those feared corrections and recessions.

Related: 'Time will tell whether that was a good bet': My adviser got me a full SpaceX IPO allocation. Was I lucky?

Lost returns

On the other hand, if you leave the $300,000 invested instead of using it to pay off your mortgage, it could grow to over $1.1 million over 20 years with a 7% annual return. At a 10% annual return, the investment could grow to more than $2 million. While investment returns obviously vary, paying off your mortgage today could mean giving up roughly $1.7 million in potential investment growth over the next 20 years.

You don't seem the kind of couple to shy away from market returns. After all, for people like you who are retired and in your 60s, advisers generally advise keeping 40%-60% in stocks. You've gone the opposite direction, with 90% in stocks, and, in fairness, many wealth managers have relaxed their views on those "rules of thumb." Your house is nearly paid off, and you are still enjoying the benefits of a bull market, notwithstanding the recent bumps.

Your investment strategy - including your 90% allocation to equities and a current withdrawal rate of about 5% - is considerably more aggressive than many financial planners recommend for retirees. Because your withdrawals are expected to decline once Social Security and pension income begin, that may prove manageable. Still, it's always worth asking whether your portfolio could withstand a prolonged bear market without affecting your peace of mind.

The bigger risk you face is not a problem paying off your mortgage, but your portfolio allocation. With 90% invested in equities, your retirement income is more exposed to a prolonged market downturn than the typical retiree's portfolio. Whether to pay off the mortgage is arguably a secondary question compared with whether your investment allocation is conducive to your peace of mind over the next decade and your spending needs.

If it does, that's fine. Own it and proceed apace.

Related: I will definitely claim Social Security early. Why do so few people talk about the elephant in the room?
